questions.title: What intuitively does Rotatory Position Encoding (RoPE) encode according to Equation (1)?
questions.question_body:
In Equation (1) RoPE pixels appear as \[cos(n\theta_0),\sin(n\theta_0),...,cos(n\theta_{d/2-1}),\sin(n\theta_{d/2-1})\]. The paper states \theta_i=\theta^{-2i/d} with \theta=10000.
I am confused about why the rotation angle appears divided by β^i instead of multiplying directly.
Could someone explain how the frequency grows (or shrinks) with higher dimensions i and what effect changing θ has on the representation ability across dimensions?

Also could you walk through an example illustrating what happens when going from frame n=8606 to 46090 tokens – how do these angles scale?

Any visual intuition—such as plotting cosine‑sine pairs over time—would help.

questions.title: Why does simple linear positional interpolation cause ‘crowding’ when extending beyond a few times its original window size?
questions.question_body:
PI scales every rotary angle uniformly by λ=s where s=L′/L.
Apparently this makes nearby token positions “crowded” especially under large extensions (> 4×).
Could someone describe mathematically why many distinct positions collapse into almost identical angle vectors?
And practically how this crowding translates into poorer perplexity / attention discrimination observed experimentally?

questions.title: What two kinds of non‑uniformity were identified in LongRoPE’s analysis and how do they differ mathematically?
questions.question_body:
The paper talks about “non‐uniformities” over RoPE dimensions and over token indices.
I understand vaguely that higher‑frequency dimensions need less scaling whereas later tokens should receive lesser interpolation.
Could someone give concrete examples:
-- For width d=4096, suppose dimensional index i=20 versus i=2000 – what heuristic describes their required lambda?
-- For token position n=10 versus n=15 000 – what criterion decides whether initial tokens should stay unchanged?

Any simplified table or diagram would clarify these two axes.

questions.title: How were the bounds for λ_i chosen for evolutionary search ([1 to s×1.25] stepping 0.01)?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4 B Search Space λ_i ranges from 1 → s·1.25 where s=L′/L.
Common sense says PI sets λ=s exactly, so why allow larger values ↑ s·1.25?
Could you explain:
– What happens if λ exceeds s?
– Why step size δλ = 0.01 was chosen instead of coarser increments/generically finer decimals?

Is there evidence that “excess” interpolation actually improves performance above naive linear scaling?

questions.title: Why enforce monotone non‑decreasing constraint λ_i ≤ λ_{i+1} during evolutionary optimisation?
questions.question_body:
The algorithm discards any candidate violating λ_i ≤ λ_{i+1}
and claims NTK theory explains it.
Can someone translate this theoretical claim:
– higher‑frequency (small‐index) dimensions should get smaller                              interpolations;
eliminate confusing intuitive reasoning:
derive relation between β^i growth rate, effective frequency f_i∝β^{-i},                           and bounds imposed.
Does this restriction really reduce evaluation cost quantitatively?

questions.title: Can you detail mutation & crossover operators used in LongRoPE’s evolution algorithm?
